content: Bullous pemphigoid is a dermatological condition that manifests as large, fluid-filled blisters on the skin. These blisters, also known as bullae, are typically found on the arms, legs, or torso. In approximately one-third of cases, individuals may also develop blisters inside the mouth. The blisters can rupture, leading to the formation of ulcers or open sores. Symptoms of bullous pemphigoid can vary widely. Some individuals may remain asymptomatic, while others may experience mild redness and irritation. In more severe cases, multiple blisters may develop. Additional symptoms can include intense itching, rashes, mouth sores, and bleeding gums. The exact cause of bullous pemphigoid remains unknown. However, it is believed to be associated with immune system dysfunction, certain underlying diseases, or the use of specific medications. This condition predominantly affects elderly individuals and is rare in younger populations. Symptoms may fluctuate over time, and in most cases, the disease resolves within six years. To diagnose bullous pemphigoid, healthcare providers may perform blood tests or a biopsy of a skin lesion. It is important to seek medical attention if you develop unexplained blisters on your skin or if you have an itchy rash that persists despite home treatments. Treatment for bullous pemphigoid often involves the use of potent anti-inflammatory medications known as corticosteroids. These may be administered orally, via injection, or as topical creams for early-stage disease. In some cases, immunosuppressive medications or chemotherapy agents may be prescribed to control the immune response. Antibiotics, such as tetracyclines, can be effective in mild cases, and niacin (a B-complex vitamin) is sometimes used in conjunction with tetracyclines. Bullous pemphigoid generally responds well to treatment, and many patients can discontinue medication after several years. However, the disease may occasionally recur after treatment is stopped. The most common complication of bullous pemphigoid is skin infection, which can arise from the open sores or ulcers caused by ruptured blisters.
